errors.problem: the tap gloss on the model answer كَانَتِ الرِّحْلَةُ طَوِيلَةً shows the sense of another sentence: the trip was 'long', not 'tall', and the -an ending here follows كَانَتْ, not 'is not'

errors.current: Fifty pounds. The road is very crowded today.
errors.problem: the Arabic الطَّرِيق مُزْدَحِم الْيَوْم has no جِدًّا; the English adds 'very', so the learner matches 'very' to nothing
errors.fix: Fifty pounds. The road is crowded today.

errors.problem: the course teaches (cafe, appointment, restaurant mistakes) that a direct object takes -an, and marks it on مَاءً, فُسْتَانًا, مَوْعِدًا, دَوَاءً, but leaves it off tāʾ-marbūṭa objects in mid-sentence: قُبَّعَة وَمَاءً (one object marked, the other not, in the same line), سَأَشْتَرِي قُبَّعَة جَدِيدَة, أَشْتَرِيَ هَدِيَّة لِآدَم, وَجَدُوا حَقِيبَة زَرْقَاء; the inconsistency contradicts the rule the mistakes sections teach
errors.fix: خُذْ قُبَّعَةً وَمَاءً كَثِيرًا (and قُبَّعَةً جَدِيدَةً, هَدِيَّةً لِآدَم, حَقِيبَةً زَرْقَاءَ)
errors.alsoChange: transliteration follows; segs glosses can add '(object form)' as in فُسْتَانًا

errors.current: sāʿa is feminine, so 'possible' takes A / at: mumkina.

errors.fix: render a bare ة as 'ة (tāʾ marbūṭa)' or leave the letter untransliterated

errors.path: scene appointment-time caption (الِانْتِظَار); scene appointment-time spots[12].ar (الِاسْتِقْبَال)

errors.path: scenarios[0].dialogue.lines[2].ar; scenarios[0].dialogue.lines[6].ar; scene morning-routine spots[2].ar (and every other شَاي / الشَّاي)

errors.problem: engine quirk: a name after the clitic لِ is capitalised as one word ('Liʾādam' for li-Ādam), the suffix ـُكُمْ comes out as '-Ukum', and the first word of an Arabic run inside English prose is capitalised mid-sentence ('and Al-bāqī', 'the meter (Al-ʿaddād)')
errors.fix: li-Ādam; -ukum; lower-case the first Arabic word when the run is mid-sentence (al-bāqī, al-ʿaddād)

notes.note: 'The tea is really very delicious' doubles the intensifier for a single جِدًّا; 'The tea is very delicious' / 'really delicious' reads better.
الْمِرْطَبَان: the dictionary vocalisation (Wehr, al-Maany) is مَرْطَبَان marṭabān with fatḥa; in Egypt the everyday word is بَرْطَمَان. Worth checking the kasra before it is taught.
اللَّبَن glossed 'the yogurt' is Levantine usage; in Egypt (the scenario's setting) laban means milk and yogurt is زَبَادِي. A short note on the spot would avoid confusion.
شَاي أَوْ قَهْوَة؟ uses أَوْ in an alternative question while directions-l5 teaches أَمْ for the same job; both are heard, but a beginner may wonder which to use.
مَبْرُوك is translated 'Enjoy it!' while its seg says 'congratulations'; the English could read 'Congratulations (on the purchase)!' so the two match.
Huda switches from dual (سَافَرْتُمَا) to singular (لَمْ تَذْهَبْ) inside one turn; grammatical, since the second question is addressed to Daniel alone, but a beginner might not notice why.
الشُّبَّاك is colloquially flavoured; the scenes teach النَّافِذَة for 'window'. Either is fine, but one word would be simpler for the learner.

notes.path: scene directions spots[10].ar; scene clothes-shop spots[7].ar; scene weather-plans spots[9].ar
notes.note: 'the railing' is labelled السُّور (lit. wall, fence) in two scenes and الدَّرَابْزِين in a third; the latter is the precise word for a railing/handrail.
الدَّرَّاجَةُ النَّارِيَّة is the only spot label carrying a final case vowel (ḍamma on الدَّرَّاجَةُ); every other label is in pause form. Style only.

the seg says 'pound (after 11–99)' under مِئَة وَعِشْرُونَ (120); the mistakes[1].why explains correctly that the noun follows the last number, so the seg could say 'pound (follows the last number, 20)'.
كُلُّ عَامٍ وَهُوَ بِخَيْر is a third-person adaptation of the fixed phrase كُلُّ عَامٍ وَأَنْتَ بِخَيْر; it is understandable, but the learner should also meet the standard second-person form.
الْمِنْضَدَة is 'table' in most dictionaries; for a café counter people usually say الْكَاوْنْتَر or الطَّاوِلَة; acceptable as is.

summary: Read the whole scenarios-1 export (16 scenarios: intros, dialogues, mistakes, quizzes and all photo-scene spots) line by line, checking harakat, case and tanwīn, gender/number agreement, verb moods after لَمْ / لَنْ / أَنْ, number–noun rules, every English line, every seg and tap gloss, every answer key and every scene label. The core Arabic is in good shape: all answer keys and right/wrong pairs are correct, dual, jussive and subjunctive forms are right, the number rules (3–10 plural, 11–99 singular -an, مِئَة + singular, feminine ثَلَاث / سِتّ) are applied correctly throughout. Fourteen findings: one major (the tap gloss on the model answer طَوِيلَةً reads 'tall (f, after is not)'), nine minor content issues that are almost all tap glosses pulled from a shared dictionary and mismatching the scene or sentence (الْإِشَارَة 'pointing', الرَّصِيف 'platform', الْعَمُود 'pole', السَّاعَة without 'clock', حَارّ 'weather', spurious '(of)', لَا always 'no'), one added 'very' in a translation, one inconsistent tanwīn on tāʾ-marbūṭa objects against the course's own taught rule, and four engine quirks reported once each. Twelve notes cover register, Egyptian vs Levantine vocabulary and style.
